SAMPLE SIZE.evidence_source: Study X: "an ethnically diverse sample of 815 undergraduates." Griskevicius, Cialdini, and Kenrick (2006): "N = 91; 61% female." Clegg et al. (2011): "sample of 236 visual artists (64% female)." Beaussart et al. (2012): "more than 700 college students (85% female)." For Beaussart et al. (2012), the value is inferred as 700 from "more than 700".

ES.evidence_source: No Pearson r (correlation coefficients) between intelligence scores and creative achievement (CAQ or ICAA) were explicitly reported in the text for any study.

Effects.evidence_source: No correlation coefficients between intelligence and creative achievement were found for any study, therefore the number of effects is 0 for each study.

Mage.evidence_source: Mean age of participants was not explicitly stated for any of the studies.

Measure IQ.evidence_source: For Study X, "general cognitive ability" was mentioned as a predictor, but no specific assessment tool or scale name for IQ or intelligence was provided. For other studies, no IQ measures were mentioned.

IQ modality.evidence_source: The modality of the intelligence measure (e.g., 'figural', 'verbal', 'both') was not specified for any study.

IQ Aspect.evidence_source: Study X: "general cognitive ability" was assessed as a predictor, which aligns with the 'g' aspect of intelligence (higher-level general intelligence).

Creativity Measures.evidence_source: No specific creativity measures such as CAQ or ICAA were mentioned for any of the studies. Other forms of creativity assessment were described but do not match the allowed values.

Domain classified.evidence_source: Study X: "assessed the sexual attractiveness of different forms of creativity: ornamental/aesthetic, applied/technological, and everyday/domestic creativity." 'Ornamental/aesthetic' maps to 'Arts', 'applied/technological' maps to 'Technological' and 'Science', and 'everyday/domestic' maps to 'Everyday'. Clegg et al. (2011): "Artistic success was measured..." which maps to 'Arts'. Beaussart et al. (2012): "creativity activities during the last year, such as painting pictures, taking artistic photographs, writing poetry, writing an original computer program, or presenting scientific or mathematical papers." 'Painting pictures', 'artistic photographs', 'writing poetry' map to 'Arts'; 'writing an original computer program' maps to 'Technological'; 'presenting scientific or mathematical papers' maps to 'Science'.

Number of studies.evidence_source: The text describes one primary study (referred to as 'Study X') and references three other prior studies: Griskevicius, Cialdini, and Kenrick (2006); Clegg et al. (2011); and Beaussart et al. (2012).

section_summary.extract_value: This section, comprising the abstract and introduction, explores the role of creativity in mate selection, examining the sexual attractiveness of ornamental/aesthetic, applied/technological, and everyday/domestic forms of creativity. The main study (Study X) involved 815 undergraduates and investigated preferences for these creativity forms, as well as the predictive power of general cognitive ability, personality, divergent thinking, self-perceptions of creativity, and creative achievement. The text also references three prior studies: Griskevicius, Cialdini, and Kenrick (2006) with N=91, Clegg et al. (2011) with N=236, and Beaussart et al. (2012) with N>700, which collectively support the idea that creativity is a desirable mate quality and is associated with mating success, often with gender-differentiated effects.
section_summary.evidence_source: The entire abstract and introduction section.
